entry.title: SetCommit: Coordinating Parallel Token Commitments in Few-Step Diffusion Language Models

link.title: SetCommit: Coordinating Parallel Token Commitments in Few-Step Diffusion Language Models

entry.content:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate many token positions in parallel, which is exactly what makes them attractive for low-latency inference. But parallelism creates a decision that autoregressive decoding never faces: at each denoising step, which predictions should be committed, and which positions should stay revisable? This post summarizes SetCommit, a training-free commitment layer that answers this question as a set-selection problem. Code: github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit (MIT).

Why independent confidence is not enough

Most decoders commit positions independently, ranked by confidence or a related token-level score. In few-step decoding this breaks down in two ways:

  • Joint inconsistency. Tokens that look reliable one by one can be unreliable together. Committing a mutually inconsistent set leaves the model with a state it cannot repair in the few updates that remain.
  • Lost conditioning. Fixing nearby uncertain positions too early prevents them from benefiting from context revealed by later denoising steps.

The failure is not about any single token’s confidence — it is about the set. So SetCommit selects the set directly.

Method

SetCommit sits between the model forward pass and the host’s state update. It adds no forward pass, no training, and no architectural change.

  1. Risk-aware set selection. From the host’s candidate budget, SetCommit chooses a commitment set that trades off individual token reliability against a local joint commitment risk over the selected neighborhood. Rather than taking the top-k most confident positions, it prefers sets whose members are individually reliable and mutually compatible.
  2. Budget-neutral local exchanges. During denoising, newly revealed context can make an earlier commitment look vulnerable. SetCommit performs bounded local exchanges — replacing a weak earlier commitment with a more reliable alternative — while keeping the host’s net commitment quota unchanged (new_commits - remasked = upstream_quota).
  3. Host contract preservation. The selector only edits the commit/remask set. Fast-dLLM keeps ownership of its dual cache, replacement-position refresh, threshold stopping, and block boundaries; Native sampling and the entropy-bounded (EB) sampler keep their own scheduling rules. This is why SetCommit composes with system-side and schedule-side accelerators instead of competing with them.

The net-progress invariant still holds: the number of committed positions never decreases across a step, so the decoder cannot stall or regress.

Results

Evaluated with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP, and HumanEval:

  • Up to +7.4 pp accuracy / pass@1 over native decoding at 32 model evaluations.
  • 1.44–1.74x geometric-mean incremental speedups at common quality targets.
  • A representative matched-quality point: LLaDA-8B on GSM8K reaches the quality target at 48 evaluations with SetCommit vs. 64 with native decoding (73.1% → 74.2%).

Because the host quota and forward count are preserved, these gains are directly attributable to which positions are committed, not to extra compute.

Reproducing

The release includes the public selector API, the paper’s policy files, a deterministic CPU smoke test that checks the host contracts and the quota audit, and the pinned LLaDA / Fast-dLLM paired runner:

git clone https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit
cd SetCommit
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
bash scripts/run_smoke.sh

The smoke test needs no model download. The full paired reproduction installs requirements-cu121.txt and fetches model weights separately.

Caveats and next steps

These are research-evaluator numbers on two model families and four benchmarks; serving-side latency (TTFT/ITL) under real batching is still open. Natural next steps are extending coordinated commitment to other parallel-decoding regimes and combining it with schedule-side budget allocation more tightly.

If you work on diffusion LLMs or efficient decoding, I’d be glad to hear your thoughts — issues and PRs welcome.
entry.summary: A training-free commitment layer for diffusion LLMs — up to +7.4 pp accuracy at 32 model evaluations, and 1.44–1.74x geometric-mean speedups at matched quality.

entry.title: ASD: Trading a Bounded Regret Budget for Faster Speculative Decoding

link.title: ASD: Trading a Bounded Regret Budget for Faster Speculative Decoding

entry.content:
Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a small draft model propose tokens that a large target model verifies in parallel. But the standard acceptance rule is stricter than it needs to be — and the waste is measurable. This post summarizes the design of ASD (Approximate Speculative Decoding), a bounded-regret acceptance policy, and what it buys in practice. Code: github.com/Kissmetothemoon/ASD (Apache-2.0).

The inefficiency of strict verification

Under strict greedy verification, the first draft token that disagrees with the target model’s argmax discards the entire remaining draft suffix. In practice, many rejected tokens are nearly as good as the argmax — the target logit gap is tiny — yet they take the whole suffix down with them. The draft model’s work is wasted, and the mean accepted length (hence throughput) suffers.

A bounded-regret acceptance policy

ASD relaxes the rule: a draft token is accepted when its regret — the gap between the target’s top logit and the target’s logit on the draft token — keeps the running total within a per-request bounded budget B. The budget is spent as accepted tokens accumulate regret, and clamps at zero.

The key property: at B = 0, ASD exactly recovers strict verification — not approximately, but token-for-token identical (verified at 0% drift on 1,319 GSM8K requests). The default configuration is therefore lossless; any quality/speed trade-off is an explicit, quantified opt-in.

Engineering constraints

Three design decisions kept the integration honest:

  • Zero-intrusion adapter. The ASD adapter returns the same (correct_len, bonus, cap_trim_lens) tuple as the native greedy verifier. KV commit, finalization, metrics, and the next draft round are all unaware of the policy switch. With the flag unset, the code path is bit-identical to upstream.
  • No host synchronization on the hot path. The per-request regret budget lives as a device tensor, bound at the low-frequency prefill seam. The decode hot path never calls .item() — control flow stays on device.
  • Fail-loud optional dependency. The research package is lazily imported: missing package plus unset flag means fully native decoding; missing package plus set flag raises at startup, not mid-request. Unsupported runtimes (CUDA graph, overlap scheduling) are rejected at launch as well.

Measured results

Setup: Qwen3-14B with a block7 draft model, 8×NVIDIA L20 (46 GB), torch 2.8.0+cu128, temperature=0, num_speculative_tokens=7, max_new_tokens=256, fixed seed.

Arm GSM8K accuracy TPS (tok/s) Accept rate Mean accept length
strict 79.68% 66.21 48.49% 3.40
ASD, B=0 79.68% (identical) 72.60 (+9.7%) 48.49% 3.40
ASD, q25 (B=2.06) 79.45% (−0.23 pp) 75.04 (+13.3%) 51.08% 3.58

Two observations. First, even B=0 is faster than the stock strict path (+9.7%) — an engineering freebie from the adapter implementation. Second, spending a small regret budget (q25) buys another +3.4 points of throughput and lifts the accept rate by 2.6 pp, at a measured accuracy cost of 0.23 pp on GSM8K — well inside a 1.0 pp acceptance budget. Math500 shows the same direction (12.20% → 12.40%, 90.3 → 94.1 tok/s).

Caveats: these are local research-evaluator numbers on fixed-length generation (ignore_eos=true), not CI results from any serving framework; server-side TTFT/ITL benchmarks remain to be run.

What’s next

  • Server-path benchmarks (TTFT/ITL) once the target runtime supports the required CUDA kernels
  • Budget schedules beyond fixed B (e.g., quantile-adaptive budgets per request phase)
  • Applying the same bounded-regret idea to other parallel-decoding regimes

If you work on speculative decoding or serving systems, I’d be glad to hear your thoughts — issues and PRs welcome.
entry.summary: Design notes on a bounded-regret acceptance policy for speculative decoding — +13.3% tokens/s on Qwen3-14B at a cost of 0.23 pp accuracy on GSM8K.
